title: Mind Beyond Gene: Regulation of Pro-Opiomelanocortin Processing and Immune-Regenerative Dynamics
content: The neuroendocrine–immune (NEI) axis coordinates the body’s adaptive responses to stress by integrating signals from the nervous, endocrine, and immune systems to preserve physiological homeostasis. Central to this regulatory network is pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), a precursor polypeptide whose tissue-specific processing generates multiple biologically active peptides, including adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and β-endorphin. The maturation of POMC is tightly controlled by prohormone convertases (PCs), primarily PC1/3 and PC2, whose expression and activity are profoundly influenced by both physiological and psychological factors, including stress-induced epigenetic modifications. This review examines psychological stress, environmental factors and metabolic cues regulate POMC expression and its enzymatic cleavage by PCs, focusing on the modulation of ACTH production, the balanced synthesis of ACTH and β-endorphin, and the physiological roles of POMC-derived peptides. Furthermore, it evaluates the immunomodulatory functions of ACTH and β-endorphin in inflammation, lymphocyte proliferation, and immune homeostasis. The differential effects of stress and relaxation on PC1/3 and PC2 expression are discussed, along with the contrasting influences of glucocorticoids and β-endorphin on stem cell function and tissue regeneration. Understanding the complex interplay among psychological states, PC activity, and peptide-mediated cellular responses provides deeper insight into the mind-gene interface and its implications for regenerative biology and immune health.
